To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

international outsourcing can lead to higher wages and lower profits in the outsourcing sector, but to lower wages and higher profits in the non-outsourcing sector, depending on the degree of outsourcing and the relative factor intensities in the two sectors.

(1) international outsourcing is likely to benefit the owners of the factors that are relatively more mobile across firms, (2) international outsourcing may benefit the owners of factors that are relatively less mobile across firms, depending on the degree of specialization, and (3) international outsourcing is more likely to benefit the factor owners who are relatively more mobile within firms.

international outsourcing is likely to have a positive distributional effect in the case of diversified equilibria and a negative distributional effect in specialized equilibria, and that in the case of partial outsourcing the distributional effect is ambiguous.

the following questions.
three questions: What is the effect of international outsourcing on the distribution of income between the two factors?
the effects of international outsourcing on the distribution of income and welfare in a two-factor, two-sector model of production.

international outsourcing is a mixed blessing for the home economy.
the effects on the distribution of income are ambiguous.

the distributional effects depend on the degree of substitutability between the two factors, the degree of substiturability between the two sectors, and the degree of substituability between the two types of production technology.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the effects of international outsourcing are ambiguous.
outsourcing is a double-edged sword.
international outsourcing can have a negative effect on wages and a positive effect on profits, and vice versa.

the distributional consequences of international outsourcing are ambiguous.
international outsourcing can have both positive and negative distributional effects.
the welfare and distributional effects are not unambiguously negative.
